posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: Why I built a clinic ERP for single-doctor practices — and what it taught me about rebuilding software right the second time
posts.desc: The origin story behind OPD ERP — why solo practitioners are stuck between paper registers and bloated hospital software, and the v1-to-v2 rebuild that taught me when to scrap working code.
posts.intro: Solo doctors don't need a hospital ERP. They need the same journey, without the overhead.
posts.content:
The gap nobody was filling. Small clinics and solo practitioners are stuck between two bad options: paper registers and spreadsheets, or enterprise hospital ERPs built for multi-department hospitals — expensive, bloated, and mostly irrelevant to a single doctor's day. A solo practice still runs through the full patient journey — registration, appointment, queue, consultation, prescription, billing, dispensing — it just doesn't need the organizational overhead of a big hospital system on top of it. The goal for OPD ERP was something lightweight enough for a solo practitioner, but powerful enough to grow into a multi-doctor clinic, a pharmacy-integrated setup, or a diagnostic centre.


v1 → v2: scrapping working code on purpose

v1 was a working Express system with dual Prisma schemas and a proxy pattern between an apps/api and an apps/auth-api. It worked — but the split architecture meant schema duplication and duplicated auth logic every time something changed. I made the deliberate call to tear it down and rebuild as v2: a single unified NestJS backend instead of two services quietly drifting apart. Before deleting v1, I captured its full spec in PROJECT_BLUEPRINT.md so none of that institutional knowledge got lost in the rewrite. v2 was then built incrementally and transparently — bare scaffolding, then validation/forms/UI kit, then branding, then role-based dashboards, then POS, then the full business logic. Sometimes the right move is deleting code that works, because the architecture underneath it won't scale cleanly.


The journey, end to end

Walk-in / Scheduled → Registration → Appointment → Token Queue → Consultation → Prescription → Lab / Radiology / Procedure Orders → Billing / POS → Pharmacy Dispensing.


A few things make this feel like a real clinic tool instead of a CRUD demo. The token queue auto-refreshes live and drives a public waiting-room display board. One login produces five completely different apps — a receptionist gets a fast POS-style terminal, a doctor gets a consult workspace, a patient gets a portal, and admin gets a full back-office dashboard. Prescriptions come with drug-catalog search, substitution tracking, allergy flags, and auto-generated lab/radiology orders straight from the consult screen. Billing has a discount engine, multiple payment modes, and a refund audit trail. And underneath all of it sits RBAC done properly — granular resource:action permissions per endpoint, JWT access/refresh tokens with rotation and theft detection. There's even a small developer platform — a live schema explorer and module registry — a very 'built by developers, for the developers who maintain it' touch.


Decisions worth explaining

  • NestJS + Prisma, one schema — a single source of truth beat premature service-splitting at this scale.
  • TanStack Router over Next.js — file-based routing without SSR overhead the app doesn't need.
  • Role-based routing as architecture — pathless layouts per role (_dashboard, _pos, _doctor, _receptionist, _patient, _developer) instead of one dashboard with conditional rendering. Cleaner mental model, better UX per role.
  • Booking ≠ waiting — an appointment never puts a patient in the live queue; only checking them in does. A small distinction, but it's the difference between the queue reflecting who's actually waiting versus everyone with a future booking.
  • Doctor-level data scoping — a doctor should never see another doctor's patients or prescriptions, retrofitted deliberately rather than assumed.

What's not done yet

The queue currently polls — no WebSocket layer yet. There's no payment gateway integration, no multi-branch/multi-clinic scoping, and no automated test suite or CI. Some endpoints still lack auth guards and are open by default — a known gap, not swept under the rug.


Who it's for

Solo practitioners who want one tool instead of five. Small multi-doctor clinics. Pharmacy-integrated practices that want prescribe → dispense → bill without manual handoffs. Diagnostic centres that need lab/radiology/procedure order tracking.


Building this taught me the real tradeoff isn't 'ship fast' versus 'rebuild right' — it's knowing which one the current version of the problem actually needs. v1 shipped fast and taught me exactly where it would break under real weight. v2 is where that lesson got applied. Next: real-time queues, payments, and multi-clinic support.
posts.footer: OPD ERP is live at opd.codymitra.com. The pre-rewrite spec that survived the v1 deletion lives on as PROJECT_BLUEPRINT.md.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: Account ERP Project
posts.desc: An accounting and finance ERP module — part of the same product suite as OPD ERP and CodyERP. Ledgers, invoicing, and financial reporting, currently in active development.
posts.intro: Accounting & finance ERP — in active development
posts.content:
Why another ERP module?. OPD ERP handles the clinical side of the CodyMitra suite — registration, queues, consultations, pharmacy. Money still needed a home. Account ERP is the accounting and finance module for the same product family: ledgers, invoicing, expense tracking, and financial reporting that the other apps in the suite can eventually plug into.


It's a standalone repo right now, deliberately scoped small so I can get the core accounting primitives — chart of accounts, journal entries, double-entry balancing — right before wiring it into OPD ERP's billing data or CodyERP's restaurant POS.


What's being built

  • Chart of accounts — configurable account hierarchy per business type.
  • Journal entries — double-entry bookkeeping with automatic balancing checks.
  • Invoicing — generate, send, and track invoice status.
  • Reports — P&L, balance sheet, and cash flow rolled up from the ledger.

Same stack discipline as the rest of the suite — TypeScript end to end, Postgres as the source of truth, and a schema I'm trying hard not to have to migrate twice.
posts.footer: Account ERP is in active development — code and progress live on GitHub.

posts.author: Priyanshu Chourasia
posts.title: ERP: What is it? What do I understand of it.
posts.desc: A personal take on what ERP actually means, after building two of them — the parts nobody tells you about until you're knee-deep in a schema.
posts.intro: Enterprise Resource Planning, from the inside
posts.content:
ERP, before I built one. Before OPD ERP, 'ERP' was just a word from business-school slides — Enterprise Resource Planning, some big SAP-shaped thing companies bought and complained about. After building two of them, I understand it very differently.


It's not one app — it's a shared source of truth

An ERP isn't a CRUD app with more tables. It's several apps — registration, billing, inventory, pharmacy, accounting — that all have to agree on the same state at the same time. The hard part was never the forms; it was making sure a token status change in the queue, a stock decrement in the pharmacy, and a line item in an invoice all stay consistent without three separate services quietly disagreeing.


What actually makes it 'enterprise'

  • Role-native interfaces — a receptionist, a doctor, and a pharmacist should never see the same screen. Each role needs its own workflow, not a shared dashboard with permissions hiding buttons.
  • Granular access control — resource:action permissions on every endpoint, not a single admin/user toggle.
  • Auditability — every state change (a prescription edit, a refund, a journal entry) needs a trail, because someone will eventually ask 'who changed this and when.'
  • Module boundaries that don't leak — Account ERP has to be able to read OPD ERP's billing data someday without becoming tightly coupled to it.

What I got wrong at first

I started OPD ERP thinking the schema was the whole job. It's maybe a third of it. The rest is workflow — modelling a token that moves through five real-world states, or a prescription that can be partially dispensed and later returned. That's where most of my redesigns happened, not in the database.


Account ERP is where I'm applying that lesson from day one — smaller scope, double-entry correctness before features, and a schema I'm trying not to migrate twice.
